html:
In August 1972 Idi Amin, military ruler of Uganda, ordered the country's South Asian minority to leave within 90 days. About 80,000 people were expelled.

Most were descendants of Indians who came in British times, some as workers on the Uganda Railway and many more as traders. Many came from Gujarat. They ran much of Uganda's commerce, and resentment of their wealth was widespread. Amin claimed he had dreamed the order and called it an "economic war". Their shops, factories and homes were seized and handed to soldiers and supporters, most of whom had no experience running them. The economy collapsed.

About 27,000 went to Britain, where many settled in Leicester and London. Several thousand went to Canada, and others to India, the United States and elsewhere. Many rebuilt successful lives, and some became leaders in business and politics in Britain. In the 1990s President Yoweri Museveni invited them back and began returning seized property; some returned.
sum: In August 1972 Idi Amin, military ruler of Uganda, ordered the country's South Asian minority to leave within 90 days. About 80,000 people were expelled.
